outline.chapter_title: Motivation and Landscape of Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
outline.description: Introduce the need for parameter-efficient adaptation of large foundation models and position orthogonal finetuning within the broader PEFT ecosystem.
subtopics: Why finetuning foundation models is hard: scale, cost, and data constraints
Three PEFT families: model finetuning, adapters, and prompts
Design goals for PEFT: parameter budget, stability, generalization, and no added latency
LoRA vs OFT at a glance: additive low-rank vs multiplicative orthogonal updates
Limitations that motivate BOFT: OFT parameter count and block sparsity biases

outline.description: Develop the linear algebra and optimization tools needed to understand OFT/BOFT and their training dynamics.
subtopics: Orthogonal matrices: angle and norm preservation; spectral properties
Cayley transform: enforcing orthogonality via skew-symmetric parameters
Neurons as column vectors: preserving pairwise angles during finetuning
Spectral norm and training stability: why preserving ||W||2 matters
Complexity notions: parameter count O(d^2), O(d log d), memory vs compute trade-offs

outline.chapter_title: Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT): Principles, Variants, and Limitations
outline.description: Explain OFT’s core idea—left-multiplying pretrained weights by a learned orthogonal transform—along with block-diagonal parameterization and its trade-offs.
subtopics: OFT forward pass: z = (R W0)^T x; zero-initialization via R = I
Cayley parameterization for R and skew-symmetric Q
Block-diagonal OFT: structure, parameter budget, and expressivity
Inductive biases of block sparsity: fixed partitioning and loss of cross-block mixing
Empirical pros and cons of OFT vs LoRA

outline.chapter_title: An Information Transmission View of Matrix Factorization
outline.description: Reframe dense orthogonal matrix construction as information transmission on a layered grid, giving design principles for sparse-to-dense compositions.
subtopics: Grid model: d × (m+1) nodes; edges from factor sparsity
Dense connectivity criterion: every source reaches every sink
Minimum free edges under orthogonality constraints
Interpreting zeros: unreachable nodes and induced sparsity
Worked example: when products of sparse factors fail or succeed to be dense

outline.chapter_title: Butterfly Structures: From FFT to Efficient Orthogonal Parameterization
outline.description: Introduce butterfly networks, their role in fast transforms, and how they enable parameter-efficient dense connectivity.
subtopics: Cooley–Tukey FFT and butterfly graphs: efficient global mixing
Butterfly factor B^F(k): 2×2 block structure with diagonal sub-blocks
Butterfly component ẐB(d,k): block-diagonal assembly and recursive definition
From 2×2 to block-butterfly (b×b blocks): generalizing to 2b×2b orthogonal blocks
Ensuring orthogonality of butterfly components via Cayley transform
Complexity: O(d log d) nonzeros vs dense O(d^2)

outline.description: Present the BOFT method—its formulation, special cases, parameter counts, and how it subsumes OFT.
subtopics: BOFT definition: R(m,b) = product of m orthogonal butterfly components
Special cases: BOFT(1,b) = block-diagonal OFT; BOFT(1,d) = full OFT
Dense with fewer parameters: m = log(2d/b), b ≥ 2; b=2 gives classic butterfly
Parameter budget: 0.5 (b−1) d m effective trainable parameters
Comparison of budgets: full OFT O(d^2), block-OFT O(b d), BOFT O(d log d)
Identity initialization: composing identities at start preserves pretrained model
Zero inference cost: folding R into W0 after training

outline.description: Detail the optimization, regularization, and engineering aspects of making BOFT work reliably on large models.
subtopics: Optimization loop: parameterizing 2×2 (or 2b×2b) orthogonal blocks via Q
Multiplicative Dropout for BOFT: randomly identity-out components/blocks (p1, p2)
Learning rates and schedulers: stability considerations vs OFT/LoRA
Layer selection: which layers benefit most in LLMs, ViTs, diffusion U-Nets
Parameter budgeting across layers: allocating m and b per layer
Implementation notes: permutations, batching, mixed precision, and caching structure
Inference fusion: pre-multiplying weights, serialization, and compatibility

outline.chapter_title: Theory and Insights: Expressivity, Regularization, and Structure
outline.description: Analyze why BOFT balances expressivity and regularity, and connect to classic transforms, metric learning, and implicit biases.
subtopics: Expressivity vs OFT: BOFT’s greater coverage with the same block size
Approximating random orthogonals: error vs parameter count trends
Kaleidoscope hierarchies: alternating products of butterfly matrices and transposes
Spectral norm preservation: role in stability and generalization
Bilinear similarity view: learning R in w_i^0 R x with orthogonality constraints
Inductive bias: alignment with Fourier/Hadamard-like global mixing
Implicit regularization from sparse factorizations

outline.description: Summarize the experimental evidence that BOFT is broadly effective on vision, language, and generative models.
subtopics: Benchmarks and tasks: large ViTs, LLMs, and text-to-image diffusion
Baselines: full finetuning, LoRA and variants, OFT block-diagonal, adapters
Metrics: accuracy/perplexity/FID or downstream alignment measures
Results overview: BOFT’s accuracy–parameter trade-off improvements
Ablations: effects of m, b, and multiplicative dropout
Stability analysis: training smoothness and convergence behavior
Approximation study: 512×512 orthogonal matrix fitting curves

outline.description: Provide actionable advice for choosing hyperparameters, integrating BOFT in pipelines, and troubleshooting.
subtopics: Choosing m and b under parameter budgets and d
Where to apply BOFT in transformers (attention vs MLP) and diffusion U-Nets
Default settings by modality and model scale
Combining BOFT with quantization (e.g., QLoRA) or other PEFT methods
Runtime and memory: training overhead vs inference parity
Debugging tips: orthogonality drift, NaNs in Cayley inversion, numerical tweaks
Worked example: 8-dimensional layer with m=3, b=2—shapes and parameter counts

outline.description: Explore generalizations of BOFT and its relationship to other structured parametrizations and network topologies.
subtopics: BOFT generalization R^G: alternating products and full orthogonal group coverage
Hybrid designs: mixing butterfly with low-rank (LoRA) updates
Alternative structured matrices: Monarch, Pixelated Butterfly, and permutations
Beyond butterfly: other information transmission topologies from networking
Automatic structure selection: learning sparsity patterns and depths
Connections to metric learning and kernel approximations

outline.description: Candidly assess BOFT’s current drawbacks and promising research directions.
subtopics: Training-time overhead from multiple sparse factors
Scalability to arbitrary d (non-powers of two) and padding strategies
Optimal selection of m and b per layer: theory and heuristics
Provable approximation bounds and sample complexity
Potential failure modes: over-regularization or underfitting on niche tasks
Hardware-aware designs: exploiting sparsity patterns for acceleration
Benchmark gaps and reproducibility considerations

outline.description: Recap the core ideas, why BOFT works, and when to use it.
subtopics: BOFT’s central insight: factorize dense orthogonal updates via butterfly components
Parameter-efficiency: O(d log d) vs O(d^2) with dense connectivity
Generalization benefits from orthogonality and structured inductive bias
Practical viability: extensive results across vision, language, and generative tasks
Actionable guidance: default hyperparameters, fusion for zero-latency inference
Future outlook: better topologies and automated structure learning
